q.intro.text: A cube-shaped gift box holds exactly sixty-four one-inch cubes: sixty-four cubic inches.

q.ask.text: How long is each edge of the box?

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the picture moves first, then the notation.

e.s1.text: Laid flat, the sixty-four cubes make one square layer, eight by eight. Its side is the square root: the square root of sixty-four is eight.

e.s2.text: In the box they stack in layers of four by four, sixteen cubes. Four layers fill it: sixteen times four is sixty-four.

e.s3.text: Count along one edge: four cubes. The edge is four inches.

e.s4.text: Check: four times four times four is sixty-four. So the cube root of sixty-four is four. The little three means: one number, used three times.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is the edge four inches, and not eight?

e.w-ok.text: Yes. Eight times eight is sixty-four, but that uses eight twice: that is the flat layer. A cube uses its edge three times, and eight times eight times eight is five hundred twelve.

e.w-sq.text: The little three changes the question: which number, used three times, makes sixty-four? An eight-inch box would hold five hundred twelve cubes.

e.w-div.text: Sixty-four divided by three is twenty-one and a third, and a box with that edge would hold over nine thousand cubes. A cube root is not dividing by three.

t.intro.text: A bigger cube-shaped box holds two hundred sixteen one-inch cubes. The cubes are stacked for you.

t.count.text: How long is one edge of this box?

t.fill.text: Type a number in the box first.

t.c-ok.text: Yes: six cubes along the edge, so the edge is six inches.

t.c-div.text: That divides two hundred sixteen by three. Count the cubes along one bottom edge instead.

t.c-other.text: Count the cubes along one bottom edge of the box.

t.check.text: Check it by cubing: six times six times six is what?

t.k-ok.text: Yes: six times six times six is two hundred sixteen. The edge, used three times, makes the volume.

t.k-mult.text: Six cubed is not six times three. It is six times six times six: first thirty-six, then two hundred sixteen.

t.k-sq.text: Six times six, thirty-six, is one layer. There are six layers: thirty-six times six.

t.k-other.text: Multiply six times six first, then times six again.

t.write.text: Tap the chips to write it with a root sign.

t.w-ok.text: Yes: the cube root of two hundred sixteen is six, because six cubed is two hundred sixteen.

t.w-sq.text: That is the square root sign. A cube needs the root with the little three.

t.w-div.text: Seventy-two is two hundred sixteen divided by three. The cube root is the edge: six.

t.w-other.text: Root sign first, then the volume under it, then the edge.

t.bound.text: One more. A box holds two hundred cubic inches. Between which two whole numbers is its edge?

t.b-ok.text: Yes: two hundred is between one hundred twenty-five and two hundred sixteen, so the cube root of two hundred is between five and six. This edge is not a whole number of inches.

t.b-sq.text: Fourteen and fifteen bound the square root of two hundred. For a cube, use cubes: five cubed is one hundred twenty-five, and six cubed is two hundred sixteen.

t.b-cubes.text: Those are the cubes around two hundred. Their cube roots are the bounds.

t.b-other.text: Which cubes sit just below and just above two hundred? Try five cubed and six cubed.

t.cb-right.text: At the start you picked four inches, and you were right. Now you can show why.

t.cb-sq.text: At the start you picked eight inches: that is the side of the flat layer, the square root of sixty-four. The box's edge is the cube root: four inches.

t.cb-div.text: At the start you picked twenty-one and a third inches: that divides by three. The edge is four inches, since four times four times four is sixty-four.

p.intro.text: Jordan writes: the square root of forty-nine is plus or minus seven, because negative seven squared is forty-nine too.

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument and see where it leads.

p.prove.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.c1.text: x squared equals forty-nine has two solutions, x equals seven and x equals negative seven,

p.c2.text: but the symbol, the square root of forty-nine, names only seven,

p.c3.text: so x is plus or minus the square root of forty-nine, plus or minus seven, and Jordan's line is wrong.

p.x-pm.text: That is Jordan's idea, the one being tested. The symbol names one number; the equation has two solutions.

p.x-pos.text: Check it: negative seven times negative seven is positive forty-nine. So negative seven is a solution of the equation.

p.x-other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the picture backs every one. The equation has two solutions; the root sign names one.
